Report:
A factory monitoring prototype receives readings from 200 temperature sensors every second. One worker validates each reading, writes it to a database, and sends alerts. During bursts, requests wait and some clients retry. The team needs timely alerts, bounded memory, and predictable recovery after failures.

The service runs on one small computer with four CPU cores and limited memory. Each request contains a sensor identifier, a sequence number, a timestamp, and a temperature. The worker opens a database transaction for every reading and waits for it to finish before processing another request. Alert delivery also runs in this worker and can wait on a slow network connection.

Sensors reconnect together after a network outage. Each reconnecting sensor sends its stored readings before returning to live measurements. Recent readings and historical readings currently enter the same first-in, first-out queue. During one replay experiment, live readings waited behind older data, but the team did not record percentile latency, queue depth, or database timings. The observations therefore do not establish which operation dominates response time.

Clients retry a request when its response times out. A retry can contain the same sensor identifier and sequence number as the original request. The database does not currently reject duplicates. Acknowledgements are sent after the database transaction, so a lost acknowledgement may cause an already stored reading to be submitted again.

The next version must remain understandable to a small team. It may use a bounded queue, a connection pool, and a limited number of workers, but it should not require a distributed platform. The team is considering small database batches and a separate alert worker. It must decide how to reject excess traffic, preserve useful ordering, prevent historical traffic from starving, and recover safely after a process restart. These readings support maintenance reports; they do not control safety equipment.

Report:
A factory monitoring prototype receives readings from 200 temperature sensors every second. One worker validates each reading, writes it to a database, and sends alerts. During bursts, requests wait and some clients retry. The team needs timely alerts, bounded memory, and predictable recovery after failures.

Purpose and boundaries. The readings support maintenance reports and help technicians investigate unusual operating conditions. They do not operate machinery, provide emergency shutdowns, or replace independent safety equipment. The engineering team has two developers and one technician available for this iteration. It wants an improvement that can be inspected, tested, and operated on a single computer. Distributed databases, orchestration clusters, and automatic scaling are outside the initial scope. The design should make later changes possible without requiring those systems now.

Hardware and deployment. The service and database share a computer with four CPU cores, eight gigabytes of memory, and a solid-state drive. A separate reporting application also uses this machine during working hours. The service runs as one process with one request-processing worker. A process supervisor can restart it after failure, but a restart does not restore items that were only held in memory. The team has not measured how much memory belongs to queued requests, database buffers, or the reporting application. No resource limit has yet been selected from evidence.

Request format. Every reading contains a sensor identifier, a sequence number, a device timestamp, a temperature value, and a firmware version. The server adds its receipt time. Some sensors have inaccurate clocks, so device timestamps alone cannot reliably describe network delay or arrival order. Sequence numbers are ordered within a device session but may restart after a device reset. The current protocol does not include a session identifier. The team needs an explicit identity rule before assuming that any pair of fields is a safe duplicate key.

Current processing path. The worker parses the request, validates the fields, opens a database connection, creates a transaction, inserts one row, commits the transaction, and closes the connection. It then checks whether the reading should create an alert. If an alert is needed, the same worker contacts an external notification service before returning its response. All requests take this path, including readings submitted for historical reporting. The implementation is easy to follow, but every blocking operation delays the next request. The report does not contain timings that identify the most expensive operation.

Normal traffic. Most sensors submit approximately one reading per second. Their schedules are not perfectly aligned, and the team has observed short clusters of arrivals. A few devices submit additional readings while technicians investigate a problem. Average traffic rate is therefore an incomplete description of the workload. The next test should preserve the arrival times of requests rather than assuming that every client waits for the previous response before sending another reading. Both a steady workload and a controlled burst would be useful, provided their parameters are recorded.

Reconnect behavior. Sensors keep a small local history during a network outage. When connectivity returns, they upload that history before resuming their normal schedule. A switch restart can cause many sensors to reconnect together. These older readings are useful for maintenance reports, but they should not delay recent observations indefinitely. At present, historical and recent readings share one unbounded first-in, first-out queue. The team has observed delays during a replay but has not measured queue age by traffic class. It cannot yet quantify how much recent traffic is affected.

Client retries and duplicates. A client retries after a response timeout because it cannot tell whether the server committed the original reading. If the commit succeeds but the acknowledgement is lost, the repeated request may insert a duplicate. If the client retries immediately during a burst, it also adds work when the service is already overloaded. The team is considering bounded retries with increasing delays, but the server must still define duplicate handling. A duplicate response should be distinguishable from a new accepted reading without requiring the client to guess what happened.

Ordering and fairness. Historical reports need a clear ordering within each sensor session; there is no stated requirement for one global order across all sensors. A future worker pool could complete requests in a different order from their arrival. Giving every recent reading strict priority could make a historical upload wait indefinitely during sustained live traffic. The team wants a policy that keeps recent observations responsive while allowing historical work to make visible progress. It is considering separate queues, a fixed share of capacity, or priority that changes with waiting time. No policy has been selected.

Database proposals. Reusing connections could remove repeated setup work, while small batches could reduce transaction overhead. Larger batches may also keep a reading waiting before its write begins. The proposed batching rule therefore needs both a maximum item count and a maximum waiting time. The database already has indexes used by reports, and adding a duplicate-detection index would affect both correctness and write cost. Any performance comparison must use the same indexes and durability settings. The team does not want an apparent speedup obtained by weakening the acknowledgement or persistence guarantee without documenting that change.

Alert delivery. The notification service occasionally responds slowly or returns an error. Moving alerts to a separate worker would keep that delay out of the main request path, but it introduces questions about persistence, retries, and duplicate notifications. An in-memory handoff could lose an alert during a restart. A persistent handoff could survive a restart but would add database work and operational rules. Historical readings should not automatically produce a burst of stale notifications. The team must first define which readings are eligible for alerts and what users should expect after an outage.

Overload and memory. An unlimited queue allows requests to be accepted even when the service cannot complete them promptly. A bounded queue makes the limit explicit but requires a clear rejection response. Requests may also have different sizes, so an item-count limit does not necessarily bound memory closely. The team wants maximum request-body and queue limits, separate queue-wait and processing deadlines, and predictable behavior when a client disconnects. Work already committed to the database must not be described as undone merely because the client stopped waiting for its response.

Measurements and experiments. The existing logs contain arrival timestamps and error messages, but no stable request identifier connecting all processing stages. The proposed measurements include queue entry, worker start, database completion, response completion, queue depth, memory usage, and outcome. The team also wants throughput and latency distributions separated into live and historical traffic. Experiments should compare one change at a time against the same saved workload. Candidate comparisons include connection reuse, a small worker pool, bounded batching, and a scheduling policy. The report provides no measured speedup or acceptable latency threshold.

Failure and recovery tests. Planned scenarios include a slow database, an unavailable notification service, repeated client submissions, a process restart during a write, and a lost acknowledgement after a commit. For each scenario, the team should state which readings were acknowledged, which were durably stored, and which may safely be retried. A clean shutdown should stop accepting new work and use a bounded drain period. If some queued requests remain unfinished, the service needs a documented way to reject or recover them. Merely restarting successfully does not demonstrate that recovery is correct.

Release constraints. The first release should retain the current API shape wherever practical and introduce changes behind a configuration option. The team can replay a small recorded workload in an isolated test database, but it must not send duplicate maintenance notifications to real users. Configuration, schema changes, and rollback steps need to be recorded with the results. The final recommendation should separate confirmed observations from hypotheses, identify the smallest useful next experiment, and explain what evidence would justify adding more concurrency or a more complex scheduling policy.
